title:
Getting started on the
Illinois Campus Cluster
body: A practical workflow for data analysis
notes: Hi everyone, I’m from Kun Wang’s lab. We mainly do computational work, so for us, HPC is a bit like the lab bench in a wet lab—it’s where we run our analyses. Today, I’ll give you a brief introduction to the Illinois Campus Cluster and walk through the basic skills you need to run computationally intensive analyses on it.

title: Prepare files on login nodes; run jobs on compute nodes
notes:
Let’s start with what we’re actually connecting to. HPC stands for high-performance computing. A cluster is a group of connected computers, and one computer in that group is called a node. This is the official NCSA overview. Our laptop connects to the head node in the picture—the login node we’ll use in this talk.

Think of that login node as our starting point. We can organize files, edit scripts, and submit work there. It’s shared with other users, so we send the heavier analysis to compute nodes. We do that by submitting a job: a request that says what to run and how much computing power it needs. The scheduler waits until the requested resources are available, then starts the work.

The login and compute nodes can reach the same project files through shared storage. That’s why we can prepare a script in one place and run it on another node. Connecting with VS Code gives us access to those files; getting compute resources is a separate step. First, though, we need an approved account and permission to use our group’s resources.

title: Request access and confirm your allocation details
body:
Existing lab accessAsk your PI or technical contact which cluster group to join.
A new computing needStart an Illinois Computes request.
Detail to confirmUsed for
NetIDYour login identity
Slurm accountThe group’s assigned computing resources
PartitionA queue you may submit to
Project pathA folder where you have permission to save files
Research access request ↗Illinois Computes request ↗

Before connecting: get account approval, confirm these four details, and set up Duo.
notes:
If I were getting started, I’d first ask my PI or the person who manages computing for the group. If the group already uses the cluster, they can tell us which group to join and how to request access. We may hear the term investor group. That means a lab or organization that has arranged cluster resources. For a new computing need, Illinois Computes is another starting point. Submitting a form starts the process; we still need approval and account setup before we can log in.

There are four details I’d keep handy. Our NetID is our login identity. The Slurm account tells the system which group’s computing resources our job can use. Slurm is the software that schedules jobs, so this account is different from our personal NetID. The partition is a queue of eligible resources. The project path is the location of a folder where we’re allowed to save files.

We need an account and partition that work together, a project folder we can write to, and Duo set up for login. The group’s technical contact can help confirm those. Throughout the examples, names such as YOUR_NETID are placeholders—we replace them with our own details. Once those are ready, we can check that the connection works.

title: The first SSH login
body:
On your laptop: open Terminal (macOS) or PowerShell (Windows)
ssh YOUR_NETID@cc-login.campuscluster.illinois.edu

ssh starts the connection · before @: your user name · after @: the cluster address

1 · Run the commandReplace YOUR_NETID, then press Enter.
2 · PasswordType your NetID password and press Enter; typing stays hidden.
3 · DuoFollow the prompt and approve the authentication request.
notes:
Let’s make the first connection from the laptop. On a Mac, we can open Terminal. On Windows, we can open PowerShell. If Windows doesn’t recognize ssh, the OpenSSH Client needs to be enabled first.

The command begins with ssh, which starts the connection. Before the at sign goes our NetID. After it goes the cluster’s address. So we replace YOUR_NETID, keep cc-login.campuscluster.illinois.edu as shown, and press Enter.

On the first connection, SSH may ask us to confirm the server’s identity. That fingerprint needs to match institutional guidance or what support confirms before we accept it. An unexpected warning that the host has changed also needs checking. Then we enter our NetID password. Nothing appears while we type—not even dots—and that’s normal. We complete the Duo prompt on our registered device. This ICC login uses our password and Duo, rather than user-created SSH keys.

A welcome message and a command prompt tell us we’re connected. The prompt means the shell is ready for a command, and commands entered here run on the cluster. The screenshot is an older official example, so its dates and quota numbers aren’t current guidance. Typing exit closes this test connection without deleting anything. Now that we know the login works, we can use the same connection through VS Code.

title: VS Code is an editor for code and project files
body:
Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is Microsoft’s code editor for working with scripts and project files.

B · ExplorerBrowse files and folders in the left sidebar.
C · EditorRead and edit scripts in the main area.
D · TerminalEnter commands in the bottom panel.
notes:
This is Visual Studio Code, usually called VS Code. It’s Microsoft’s editor for code and project files. What I find useful is having the files, the editor, and a terminal together in one window. A script is just a text file containing instructions for a program to run.

This is Microsoft’s example screenshot, so these aren’t the files we’ll be working with. B marks Explorer, where we browse files and folders. C marks the editor, where we read or change an open file. D marks the terminal, where we enter commands. That bottom panel can show other things too, but here it’s showing a terminal.

Those are the three areas we’ll use most: find a file on the left, work on it in the middle, and enter commands below. With a remote connection, the same window can work with our files on the cluster.

title: Files stay on the cluster; terminal commands run there
body:
LOCAL Your laptop
VS Code window
View and editanalysis.pyYour screen, keyboard, and mouse
Remote - SSH
⟷
View · edit · save
REMOTE The cluster
Project filesdemo/analysis.pySave updates this file.
Remote terminalCommands run on the cluster.

In the SSH window, saves update cluster files and terminal commands run on the connected host.
notes:
Here’s the part that makes VS Code convenient. The window is on our laptop, but the files can stay on the cluster. The Remote - SSH extension connects the two.

For example, suppose we open analysis.py from our remote demo folder. We see it on the laptop screen, but the file itself is demo/analysis.py on the cluster. When we press Save, we update that remote file. We don’t have to download it, edit a separate copy, and upload it again. This diagram shows where we’ll end up once we’ve uploaded the project.

The terminal in that connected window also runs on the remote host. Our first host is a login node. A separate local terminal would run commands on the laptop instead, so it matters which terminal we’re using. Later, an interactive job will give us a shell on a compute node, and we’ll check the host when we make that change.

So VS Code handles our file work, while Slurm gives the analysis its compute resources. Connecting the editor doesn’t reserve a compute node. To get this window set up, we’ll install VS Code and its Remote - SSH extension on the laptop.

title: Install VS Code and the Remote - SSH extension
body:
First: download and open VS Code on your laptop.
1
Open Extensions
Extensions icon
Left Activity BarOr Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+X
2
Search Remote - SSHChoose the Microsoft extension
3
Click InstallWait for installation to finish

The editor and Remote - SSH extension are installed on your laptop.
notes:
We need two things on the laptop: VS Code itself and the Remote - SSH extension. We download VS Code for our operating system, install it, and open it.

Inside VS Code, Extensions are add-ons that give the editor extra features. The small screenshot shows the Extensions icon in the left sidebar, also called the Activity Bar. We can click that icon, or use Command-Shift-X on a Mac and Control-Shift-X on Windows or Linux. Those keys are pressed together.

We search for Remote - SSH and choose the extension published by Microsoft. The larger screenshot is an older official example, so we don’t need that exact version. We’re looking for Microsoft as the publisher and the Install button. We install the current version and wait for it to finish.

That prepares the editor on the laptop. Python and our analysis packages will be set up separately on the cluster. To make the connection now, we’ll use the Command Palette—a searchable menu of VS Code actions.

title: Connecting VS Code with Remote - SSH
body:
1
Choose Connect to Host…Cmd+Shift+P (Mac) · Ctrl+Shift+P (Windows/Linux)
Search: Remote-SSH: Connect to Host
2
Enter your login address
Use this address:YOUR_NETID@
cc-login.campuscluster.illinois.edu

Password + Duo
Choose Linux if asked.

3
Check the SSH indicatorLower-left corner of the new window
notes:
We open the Command Palette with Command-Shift-P on a Mac, or Control-Shift-P on Windows or Linux. Then we search for Remote-SSH: Connect to Host and select it.

In the address field, we enter our NetID, an at sign, and cc-login.campuscluster.illinois.edu. YOUR_NETID is the part we replace. The address wraps across two lines on the slide to fit, but we enter it as one address. Microsoft’s screenshots show a sample host; we use the cluster address shown here.

We go through the password and Duo prompts again. If VS Code asks about the remote operating system, we choose Linux, because that’s what the cluster runs. It may open a new connected window.

The lower-left SSH indicator is our check that this worked. It should name the cluster host. If the connection seems stuck, the Remote - SSH output or login terminal may show an authentication prompt waiting for us.

Once that indicator confirms the connection, we’re ready to choose where the project files will go.

title: Choose home, project, or scratch storage
body:
LocationUse it forLimits and actions
/u/YOUR_NETIDSettings and small personal filesVery limited quota: 100 GiB (soft limit). Keep large datasets elsewhere.
/projects/YOUR_GROUPGroup data, software, and retained outputsShared group quota. Keep backups: no snapshots are kept for file recovery.
/scratch/YOUR_NETIDTemporary working dataTemporary only: files typically deleted after 30 days without access, sometimes sooner.

Use your group’s full project path; /projects/YOUR_GROUP is a placeholder.
notes:
Before putting files on the cluster, we need to choose a place for them. Home, project, and scratch storage serve different purposes.

Home is under /u, followed by our NetID. It’s for settings and small personal files. Its quota—the amount of space we’re allowed to use—is very limited: 100 GiB as the documented soft limit and 103 GiB as the hard limit. Staying above the soft limit for seven days stops new writes until we bring our usage down. This quota can’t be expanded, so home is a poor place to keep large datasets.

Project storage is shared by the group. Its capacity depends on the group’s allocation, and it’s where we can keep group data, software, and outputs. It has no snapshots, meaning saved filesystem states that could restore earlier files. Important data therefore need a separate backup plan.

Scratch is temporary working space. Files are typically deleted after 30 days without access, and sometimes sooner when space is tight. Purged files can’t be recovered, so any outputs we want to keep need to be moved elsewhere.

For this walkthrough, we’ll use the writable project location our group gives us. /projects/YOUR_GROUP is only a placeholder for that full path, just as YOUR_NETID stands for our own NetID. We’ll open the project location first, then put our demo folder inside it.

title: Open the remote project location
body:
1
File → Open FolderIn the connected VS Code window
2
Enter the destination, then OKUse your group’s full path, for example:
/projects/YOUR_GROUP
3
Confirm this window is remoteThe lower-left SSH indicator names the cluster.

Explorer now shows the remote destination.
The demo folder is still on your laptop.
notes:
We can now open that location in the connected VS Code window. We choose File, then Open Folder, enter our group’s full project path, and click OK. On the slide, /projects/YOUR_GROUP means the parent folder where we want to put demo.

Microsoft’s screenshot shows /home/sana/demo on its own example system. We use our approved project path instead. We also check that the SSH indicator still names the cluster. With that connection active, Explorer is showing remote folders.

At this point, we’ve opened the destination. The demo folder is still on our laptop, so opening the remote folder hasn’t transferred it yet. We now have somewhere to put it.

notes:
The offline package includes the small demo project we’ll use. After unzipping the package on the laptop, we can find demo inside HPC_Introduction using Finder on a Mac or File Explorer on Windows. We drag that whole demo folder into the file list in the remote VS Code Explorer. Dropping it into the file list uploads it to that destination; an open editor tab isn’t the target here.

Once the transfer finishes, we choose File, then Open Folder again, and open the uploaded demo folder. In this example that’s /projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo, with our own group’s path in place of the placeholder. The folder contains our input data and scripts: samples.csv is the small input table, analysis.py is a Python script, and hello.sbatch is a job script we’ll look at later.

We expand data and open samples.csv. A header and three sample rows are what we expect to see. That’s a quick check that the file arrived and we can read it on the cluster. From here, Command-S on a Mac or Control-S on Windows and Linux saves changes directly to the remote file.

Dragging a folder is convenient for this small project. For a large dataset, we’d use the transfer service our group recommends, such as Globus, and check that it finishes before starting the analysis. With our small project in place, we can open its terminal.

title: Open a terminal in the same project
body:
1
Terminal → New TerminalIn your remote VS Code window
hostnameWhich computer?
Expect a login node.
cd /projects/YOUR_GROUP/demoMove into your uploaded project.
Use your group’s actual path.
pwdWhich folder?
Check the full project path.

Run one line, press Enter, wait for the prompt, then continue.
notes:
So far, we’ve worked through the file interface. We’ll also need a few commands, and we can enter them in the same VS Code window. We choose Terminal, then New Terminal. The terminal is the text window we see; the shell is the program that reads our commands. In this connected window, that shell runs on the cluster.

The screenshot is Microsoft’s remote terminal example. Its uname command reports Linux. For our own session, the three checks below tell us which computer and which folder we’re using.

First, hostname prints the computer’s name. At this stage, we expect a login host, such as cc-login1. Then cd changes the current folder to our uploaded demo project. We replace /projects/YOUR_GROUP with our group’s actual path. If cd works, it usually prints nothing. Finally, pwd prints the full path of the folder we’re now in. We want that to match the demo folder open in Explorer.

We enter one line, press Enter, and wait for the prompt before entering another. The prompt tells us the shell is ready. In our examples, a dollar sign marks that prompt; we don’t type the dollar sign ourselves. These short checks are fine on the login node. The heavier analysis will go to compute resources later. Before we get there, it helps to know how to read the parts of a command.

title: Read the program, options, and path in a command
body:
head -n 5 data/samples.csv
Programhead displays the beginning of a text file.
Option + value-n 5 asks for the first five lines.
File pathdata/samples.csv is the path to the file to read.

Quotes keep a path together: head -n 5 "data/samples.csv". They are required for paths containing spaces.
notes:
Suppose we want a quick look at the start of our input table. We can use head -n 5 data/samples.csv. It’s easier to read if we take it in three parts.

head is the program. The option -n, followed by the value 5, asks for the first five lines. Then data/samples.csv is the file to read. If the file has fewer than five lines, head just shows the lines that are there.

Everything after head is an argument. Some arguments change what a command does; others give it a value or a file path. Option letters belong to individual commands, so -n can mean something different in another program.

Spaces usually separate arguments. Quotes keep a path together when it contains spaces. The quoted version shown here also works, although data/samples.csv doesn’t need quotes because it has no spaces.

There’s one more piece we need for this example: data/samples.csv is a path relative to our current folder. So before reading or running anything, we need to know where the terminal is working.

title: Use pwd and cd to move through the project
body:
Type commands after $; other lines are output
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
$ cd data
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo/data
$ cd ..
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
pwdPrint the current folder.
cd dataEnter the data subfolder.
cd ..Go up to the parent folder.

. = current folder · .. = parent folder

/projects/… starts at the filesystem root; data/… starts from the current folder.
notes:
Here we’re starting in demo, and pwd confirms its full path. In the transcript, we type the part after the dollar sign. The other lines are the computer’s output.

cd data moves into the data subfolder. It usually doesn’t print a message, so we use pwd again to see that the path now ends in demo/data. Then cd .. takes us up one level, back to demo. Another pwd confirms we’re back. Two dots mean the parent folder; one dot means the current folder.

There are two ways to write a location. An absolute path starts with a slash and gives the location from the filesystem root, like the full /projects path here. A relative path starts from wherever we are now. That’s why cd data works while we’re in demo. File and folder names are case-sensitive, so capitalization matters too.

We can move through the folder tree this way. There are also two useful shortcuts for going home and returning to where we were.

title: Use cd ~ for home and cd - to go back
body:
Continue from demo on the previous page
$ cd ~
$ pwd
/u/YOUR_NETID
$ cd -
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
cd ~Go to your home folder.
cd -Return to the previous folder and print its path.
pwdConfirm where the terminal is now.

cd .. means parent folder. cd - means previous folder.
notes:
We’re still in demo. cd ~ takes us to our home folder. The symbol is called a tilde, and here it stands for home. pwd confirms the new location as /u/YOUR_NETID, where YOUR_NETID would be our own NetID.

Now cd - takes us back to the folder we were in before. In this example, that’s demo. This command also prints its destination, which is why we see the same path again when we run pwd afterward.

The distinction is useful: cd .. goes up to the parent folder in the directory tree. cd - returns to the previous location, wherever that was. They can take us to different places.

We’ve returned to demo, so we can now inspect the names inside data while keeping the terminal right here.

title: List visible and hidden names with ls
body:
Illustrative data folder; commands run from demo
$ ls data
counts.tsv  samples.csv
$ ls -a data
.  ..  counts.tsv  samples.csv
ls dataList visible file and folder names inside data.
ls -a dataInclude hidden names beginning with a dot.

. is this folder; .. is its parent. Later, ls -a in demo will also show .venv.

counts.tsv is a larger illustrative file. The supplied demo uses samples.csv.
notes:
We’re back in demo, and now we want to see what’s inside data. That’s what ls data does. It lists the names in that folder; it doesn’t move us there.

For this example, imagine data contains a larger file called counts.tsv as well as samples.csv. That larger file is just here to help us compare file sizes in a moment. The supplied demo still uses the small samples.csv.

Plain ls shows the visible names. Add -a, and we also see names beginning with a dot. Here, one dot means this folder, and two dots mean its parent. Later, when we create our Python environment, ls -a in demo will also show its hidden .venv folder.

So now we know which names are there. To check a file’s size and other details, we can add a couple more options.

title: Show file details and readable sizes with ls
body:
-l: details · -h: readable sizes · -a: include hidden names

Illustrative listing; total lines omitted
$ ls -l data
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group 25165824 Oct 27 10:00 counts.tsv
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group       58 Oct 27 10:00 samples.csv
$ ls -lh data
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group  24M Oct 27 10:00 counts.tsv
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group   58 Oct 27 10:00 samples.csv
$ ls -lah data
drwxr-xr-x 2 user group 4.0K Oct 27 10:00 .
drwxr-xr-x 3 user group 4.0K Oct 27 10:00 ..
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group  24M Oct 27 10:00 counts.tsv
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group   58 Oct 27 10:00 samples.csv

Same file: 25165824 bytes → 24M (24 MiB). Folder size here is not the total of its contents.
notes:
Let’s use the same folder and ask ls for more detail. With -l, we get one line per entry. Reading across, there’s the file type and permissions, a link count, the owner, the group, the size, the modification date and time, and finally the name. The filename and size are usually the first things I check. The users and dates here are just examples.

Here’s why I’m using the larger counts.tsv example. In the first listing, its size is 25,165,824 bytes. That’s a bit hard to read quickly. Add -h, and the same size appears as 24M. Here that means 24 MiB, using units based on 1024. The file hasn’t changed. We’ve only changed how its size is displayed.

Our small samples.csv stays at 58 bytes, so its number looks the same. And we can combine the options: -lah gives us the details from -l, the hidden entries from -a, and the readable sizes from -h.

One thing to watch: the size shown for a folder isn’t the total size of all the files inside it. We’ll use du to check that. First, let’s see how to make a folder and copy a file.

title: Create folders with mkdir and copy files with cp
body:
CommandResult
mkdir resultsCreate one new folder.
mkdir -p results/qcCreate missing folders along the path; accept existing folders.
cp -i notes.txt notes_backup.txtCopy a file; ask before overwriting.
cp -r data data_backupCopy the folder and its subfolders to a new destination.

cp: source first, destination second. The source stays in place.

Check the result with ls. Copying a large dataset also uses extra storage.
notes:
Once we can see our files, we’ll often want to organize them. VS Code’s Explorer can do most of this too, but these commands come up a lot in instructions. They’re examples we can choose from, so we don’t need to run every line to set up the demo.

mkdir results creates a folder called results. If it already exists, plain mkdir reports an error. Add -p, as in mkdir -p results/qc, and it creates any missing folders along that path. It also accepts folders that are already there.

For cp, read the source first and the destination second. Here, notes.txt is the original, and notes_backup.txt is the copy. The -i asks before replacing a file that already has that destination name. The original stays where it is.

To copy a whole folder and its subfolders, we use -r. In this example, data_backup is a new destination for a copy of data. Copying a large dataset also uses extra storage, so it’s worth checking whether we need another copy.

These commands often finish without printing anything. We can use ls to see what changed. Once we’ve made a copy, we might want to rename it or remove it.

title: Move or rename with mv; remove a file with rm
body:
Move or rename: source first, destination second
mv -i notes_backup.txt notes_old.txt

Rename the backup; -i asks before replacing an existing destination file.

Remove the unwanted copy
rm -i notes_old.txt

-i asks before deleting. Check the filename before confirming.

Shell deletion normally has no Trash recovery. Check the result with ls.
notes:
Let’s say we’ve made notes_backup.txt and now want to call it notes_old.txt. That’s what this mv command does. As with cp, the source comes first and the destination second.

Here, both names are in the same folder, so mv renames the file. If the destination were in another folder, it would move the file there. The -i asks before replacing an existing destination.

If we no longer need that copy, rm -i notes_old.txt asks before deleting it. This is the point where I’d check the filename carefully. Shell deletion normally doesn’t put the file in the Trash, so we shouldn’t expect to recover it that way.

After either command, ls lets us check what happened. That covers moving files around. Now let’s look inside a small file without changing it.

title: Inspecting a small text file
body:
CommandUse
cat notes.txtPrint the entire small file
head -n 5 data/samples.csvPrint up to 5 lines from the start
less notes.txtBrowse text; press q to leave
Output of head for the included sample table
sample_id,reads
sample_A,1000
sample_B,1500
sample_C,1200

Preview a few rows before running the analysis. Avoid printing a huge file with cat.
notes:
Before running an analysis, I usually want a quick look at the input. cat prints the whole text file in the terminal, so it’s useful for something short, like notes.txt. For a large file, I’d start with head instead. That way, we don’t fill the terminal with thousands of lines.

In head -n 5 data/samples.csv, -n 5 asks for up to five lines from the start. Our file only has four lines, so we see all four. The first line gives the column names. Then we have three sample names and their example values, with commas separating the fields.

For a longer text file, less gives us a viewer we can scroll through. Press q to leave the viewer and return to the shell prompt. We can also open small text files directly in VS Code.

These commands are for ordinary text. Images, saved R objects, and other binary files need a suitable viewer. Once we can read a text file, the next useful thing is finding a particular file or a line inside it.

title: Find a file, then find text inside it
body:
Search filenames within data and its subfolders
find data -type f -name "*.csv"
-type f / -nameKeep files only / match their names against the pattern.
"*.csv"The * matches any text before .csv.
Search inside this file; -n includes line numbers
grep -n "sample_B" data/samples.csv
Expected grep output: line 3 contains the match
3:sample_B,1500
notes:
Sometimes we know which kind of file we want, but we don’t know exactly where it is. find can help with that.

In this command, data is where the search starts. find looks there and in its subfolders. The -type f keeps regular files in the results, and -name matches their names against a pattern. In "*.csv", the star stands for any text before .csv.

We keep that pattern in quotes so the shell passes it to find without expanding it first. In our small project, we’d expect to get data/samples.csv back.

Once we have the file, grep lets us search the text inside it. Here we’re looking for sample_B. The -n adds the line number, so 3:sample_B,1500 tells us the matching text is on line three.

Neither command changes the file. Starting the search in the relevant project folder also keeps the results manageable. We’ve found the file and a row inside it; now we can check its line count and how much storage the folder uses.

title: Count lines and check disk usage
body:
Run this command
wc -l data/samples.csv
Expected output; do not type this line
4 data/samples.csv
wc -lCount lines in this text file.
4 linesOne header plus three sample rows.
Check space used by the input folder
du -sh data

-s gives one summary total · -h uses readable units such as K or M

wc -l includes header lines. du shows space used; quota shows usage and limits.
notes:
A line count is a quick way to check a text file before running an analysis. wc -l data/samples.csv gives us four, followed by the filename. That’s one header line and three sample rows. Strictly speaking, -l counts newline characters, and all four lines in this example end with one.

We do need to know the file format before calling that a sample count. Another file might have comments, several header lines, or one record spread across multiple lines.

To check storage, we use du -sh data. The -s asks for one summary total for the folder, and -h makes the units easier to read, with sizes like K or M. The exact value can vary with the filesystem.

That tells us how much space this folder uses. quota answers the other question: how much are we using, and what limit applies? It shows the usage and limits reported by the cluster.

There are quite a few options here, and I wouldn’t try to memorize them all. It’s more useful to know how to look them up.

title: Help and everyday terminal shortcuts
body:
Command / keyWhat it does
man lsOpen the manual; press q to leave
head --helpShow the Linux command’s built-in help
TabComplete a file or folder name
↑ / historyRecall previous commands / list shell history
Ctrl+CInterrupt the command currently running in this terminal
clear / exitClear the display / leave the current shell

Keep this login shell open for job submission; exit closes it.
notes:
If I forget what an option does, I usually start with the manual or the command’s help. man ls opens the manual for ls, and q gets us out again. Many commands also have --help, like head does here. These examples are for the cluster’s Linux shell; a laptop’s version can have slightly different options.

A few shortcuts also save a lot of typing. Tab helps complete a file or folder name. The up arrow brings back a previous command, which we can check or edit before pressing Enter. history lists earlier commands.

Ctrl+C interrupts the command currently running in this terminal. It doesn’t cancel a batch job we submitted separately to Slurm. We’ll use a Slurm command for that.

clear just clears the display. exit leaves the current shell. Depending on where we are, that could leave a compute shell or close the SSH connection. For now, we’ll keep our login shell open.

We can now find, organize, and inspect the files we need. The next step is asking the cluster to run a job.

title: Slurm runs work on allocated resources
body:
LOGIN NODE
Prepare and submithello.sbatchYour terminal stays here.
sbatch→
SlurmWait for resourcesThe scheduler
Allocate→
COMPUTE NODE
Run the jobhello.sbatchThe program runs here.
↕↕
Same shared demo/ folderInput · scripts · output

Batch: submit a script. Interactive: request a compute shell with srun.

Submit on the login node; the job runs on an allocated compute node.
notes:
We’re ready to run something, but first we need the cluster to give our job some resources. That’s Slurm’s job. Slurm is the scheduling software in the middle of this diagram.

We prepare a script on the login node and send it to Slurm with sbatch. Slurm checks the request. If the resources aren’t available yet, the job waits in a queue. When they are available, Slurm allocates them, which means it reserves them for our job, and the program runs on a compute node.

Both nodes can access the same approved project folder. Our inputs, scripts, and outputs stay there, so we don’t need to copy the whole project to another computer for every run.

Our terminal stays on the login node after we submit. The batch job runs separately and can keep going even if we disconnect the laptop. Later, we’ll also request an interactive compute shell with srun, which is useful for setting up software.

For now, let’s open hello.sbatch and see what a batch request actually contains.

title: Read a Slurm batch script line by line
body:
Select a line

Use the Slurm account assigned to your group.

01Use Bash to read the commands.
02Give the job a recognizable name.
03Use the Slurm account assigned to your group.
04Use a partition that this account can access.
05Request one compute node.
06Request one task for this program.
07Reserve one CPU for that task.
08Request 1 GiB of RAM per node.
09Set a five-minute running-time limit.
10Print a message into the job output.

Edit these lines inside hello.sbatch in VS Code, then save. Submit it from the terminal after reviewing the resource settings.
notes:
Here’s the whole file for our first job. hello.sbatch is plain text. The top part tells Slurm what we need, and the command at the bottom tells the computer what to do.

The first line selects Bash to read the commands. The lines beginning with #SBATCH are settings for Slurm. We put those before the commands that run the program.

The job name helps us recognize the submission. The account identifies our group’s compute allocation, and the partition selects a queue we can use. YOUR_ACCOUNT and YOUR_PARTITION are placeholders, so we replace them with a valid pair from our group.

The next lines request one node, one task, and one CPU for that task. Then we ask for one GiB of memory per node and a five-minute running-time limit. The clock for that limit starts when the job runs; time waiting in the queue doesn’t count. Finally, echo prints the message into the job’s output.

We’ll edit and save this file in VS Code, then submit it with sbatch. Running bash hello.sbatch directly would treat the #SBATCH lines as comments and run the command on our current machine without requesting resources.

Before we submit, let’s make those node, task, and CPU settings a bit more concrete.

title: Set nodes, tasks, CPUs, memory, and time for a job
body:
Example resource request: count the node, the tasks, then the CPUs.

--nodes=11 computer
--ntasks=22 tasks in the whole job
--cpus-per-task=22 CPUs reserved for each task
Node 1One computer
Task 1One program process
CPUCPU
Task 2One program process
CPUCPU
2 tasks × 2 CPUs/task = 4 CPUs requestedntasks is already the total; do not multiply by nodes again.

Reserving resources does not launch the tasks or make the program parallel.

Keep hello.sbatch at: 1 node · 1 task · 1 CPU/task
--mem=1G1 GiB of RAM per node--time=00:05:00Runtime limit: hours:minutes:seconds
notes:
I find these settings easier to understand by counting the boxes. The big box is one node, so one computer. In this illustration, we request two tasks across the whole job. Each task represents a program process, and each one has two CPUs reserved. Two tasks times two CPUs per task gives us four CPUs in total.

The ntasks value already counts tasks across the whole job. We don’t multiply it by the number of nodes again. And a task here doesn’t mean a sample or an input file.

These boxes show the resources we’re requesting. They don’t show every CPU physically inside the computer. Depending on the system, a Slurm CPU can mean a core or a hardware thread.

Requesting resources also doesn’t automatically make a program use them. For example, python analysis.py starts one process. Running several processes needs suitable software and a launcher, and a program that uses several threads needs its own worker or thread setting.

Our actual hello job is smaller than this illustration: one node, one task, and one CPU. The --mem=1G asks for one GiB of working memory per node, separate from disk storage. The --time value is in hours, minutes, and seconds, so 00:05:00 means five minutes of running time. Queue waiting isn’t included. For a real analysis, we’d choose these values to match the software and data.

For hello, we can keep these small settings. Now we’re ready to submit it.

title: Submit the first job: hello.sbatch
body:
In the remote demo folder, after saving the file
pwd
ls hello.sbatch
sbatch hello.sbatch
Example response; record the ID returned by your submission
Submitted batch job 123456

This first job prints a message. It does not run analysis.py yet.
notes:
Let’s save hello.sbatch in VS Code first. Then, in our remote terminal, pwd confirms that we’re in demo, and ls hello.sbatch checks that the saved file is there. Once that looks right, sbatch hello.sbatch sends the job to Slurm.

The response gives us a job ID. Here it’s 123456, but we keep the number our own submission returns. It identifies this particular job, so we’ll use it to check the status and find the output.

That response means the job was accepted. It doesn’t mean the job has started or finished; it may still be waiting. This first job only prints a message. We’ll run analysis.py later.

The submission happens in the terminal after we save the file. Pressing Run in the editor doesn’t submit a Slurm job. So we’ve sent our request—now let’s see what happens to it.

title: Checking the queue and stopping a job
body:
-u selects your user; run squeue again to refresh
squeue -u YOUR_NETID
Illustration: job 123456
PD Pending Queued; check the reason
→
R Running Using allocated resources
→
No longer listed Read the output slurm-123456.out
Leaving the queue does not prove success.
Optional: cancel an unwanted job. Let hello finish here.
scancel 123456

After hello leaves the queue: cat slurm-123456.out → My first HPC job. Use your job ID.
notes:
To see our jobs, we use squeue -u YOUR_NETID, replacing YOUR_NETID with our own username. The -u selects the user. Each time we run the command, we get a new snapshot, so we run it again to check for a change.

PD means pending. The job is waiting, and the listed reason helps explain why. R means it’s running on the resources Slurm allocated. Our tiny hello job may finish before we even check.

Once it leaves the queue, we look at the output. For the example job ID, that’s cat slurm-123456.out. We use our own job ID in the filename, and we expect to see My first HPC job. Leaving the queue by itself doesn’t prove that a job succeeded. Missing or unexpected output is something we need to investigate.

If we do want to stop a submitted job, scancel followed by its job ID does that. We’ll let hello finish here. Ctrl+C in a separate log viewer only interrupts that viewer; it doesn’t cancel the batch job.

We’ve now submitted a job and checked its result. For the analysis job, we can make the log filenames clearer and ask for an email when the job ends.

title: Output files and email notifications
body:
In analysis.sbatch, before executable commands
#SBATCH --output=analysis-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=analysis-%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=YOUR_NETID@illinois.edu
Illustration: analysis job 123457. Slurm fills in %j.
Program outputOrdinary messages
→
analysis-123457.out
Program diagnosticsErrors and other messages
→
analysis-123457.err
Slurm eventsEND or FAIL
→
Email toYOUR_NETID@illinois.edu
An .err file can also contain progress messages. Read its contents.

%j becomes the job ID. Use your email address, or remove both mail lines.
notes:
These lines control where the analysis job’s messages go. They’re already in the supplied analysis.sbatch template, before the commands that load software and run the analysis.

--output names the file for ordinary program output. --error names the file for errors and other diagnostic messages. Some programs also put normal progress messages there, so an .err file doesn’t automatically mean the job failed. We need to read what it says.

The useful part of these names is %j. We leave that in the script, and Slurm replaces it with the job ID. So, for job 123457, analysis-%j.out becomes analysis-123457.out. That gives each submission its own named log.

With these filenames, the logs go into the folder we submit from. If we add a subfolder to the path, we need to create that folder before submitting.

Email is optional. --mail-type chooses the events: END when the job ends, and FAIL for failure. --mail-user gives the recipient. We put our own address there, or remove both mail lines if we don’t want email. Delivery depends on the cluster’s email setup, and we still check the results even if we receive a completion email.

That covers the usual messages and notifications. Next are two optional resource requests, starting with a GPU.

title: When the analysis needs a GPU
body:
Optional GPU job: use your group’s GPU partition and GPU type
#SBATCH --partition=YOUR_GPU_PARTITION
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:GPU_TYPE:1
Inside an allocated NVIDIA GPU job
nvidia-smi
--gresRequest GPUs with gpu:TYPE:COUNT; count is per node.
GPU_TYPE / final 1The configured GPU type / one GPU per allocated node.

The tiny demo needs no GPU. Add this only for software that supports and uses one.
notes:
Some analysis tools can use a GPU. It’s an additional processor, and the software has to support it. If our tool needs one, we first need an account and GPU partition that our group can access.

The partition line selects that GPU partition. Then --gres asks for the GPU resource. In gpu:GPU_TYPE:1, GPU_TYPE is the type name configured on the cluster, and the final 1 means one GPU per allocated node. We get the valid partition and type names from our group’s documentation or support contact.

Reserving a GPU doesn’t make a CPU-only program use it. Inside an allocated NVIDIA GPU job, nvidia-smi shows the GPU visible to the job and some basic usage information. The GPU also has its own memory, separate from the CPU RAM we request with --mem.

The software needs a compatible environment too, so we follow its installation instructions. Our small demo stays on CPUs.

Another optional request is choosing a particular compute node. A GPU type describes the hardware we need; a node name identifies a particular computer. Let’s look at that distinction next.

title: When a particular node is required
body:
Optional: use a compute-node name your account can access
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --nodelist=NODE_NAME
sinfo: inspect resources; -p selects the partition; -N lists nodes
sinfo -p YOUR_PARTITION -N
--nodes=1How many nodes you request
--nodelistWhich named node you request

Normally let Slurm choose. Name a compute node only when your group requires that machine.
notes:
A GPU type tells Slurm what hardware we need. A node name goes one step further and asks for a particular machine.

These two options are easy to mix up. --nodes=1 means “give me one computer.” --nodelist=NODE_NAME means “give me this particular computer.” NODE_NAME has to be a real compute node that our account and partition allow. A login node doesn't belong here.

sinfo lets us inspect the cluster's resources. The -p option selects a partition, and -N shows the information by node. Seeing a node in that list doesn't guarantee that our account can use it.

For most jobs, I'd let Slurm choose. Naming one machine gives the scheduler fewer choices, so we may wait longer. It can be useful when a group needs a particular machine for a test or comparison. If we just need more memory or a certain GPU type, we can usually request that resource directly.

We now have the basic resource settings. Let's use them to get a compute shell where we can prepare our software.

title: Open an interactive compute shell with srun
body:
From the login shell in demo: paste this whole block as one command
srun --account=YOUR_ACCOUNT --partition=YOUR_PARTITION \
  --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=2 \
  --mem=4G --time=00:15:00 --pty bash
srunStart a program on allocated compute resources.
--pty bashOpen an interactive terminal running the Bash shell.
After the prompt returnshostname should show a compute node; pwd should show the project folder.

A trailing \ continues a command onto the next line; nothing follows it on that line.
notes:
So far, our terminal has been on the login node. That's where we've organized files and submitted jobs. To prepare the software, we'll ask Slurm for a shell on a compute node.

We enter this command from the login shell, inside demo. --account and --partition need our approved values. The rest asks for one node, one task, two CPUs for that task, four GiB of memory, and a fifteen-minute time limit. Those are example settings for this small setup task.

This is one command spread across three lines. Each backslash joins its line to the next one, so it must be the last character on that line, with nothing after it. srun starts a program on allocated resources. Here, --pty gives us an interactive terminal, and bash is the shell we want to run.

We may have to wait for resources. Once the prompt appears, hostname should show a compute node, and pwd should still show our project folder. That tells us where the commands we type in this terminal will run.

VS Code's Run button and notebook cells don't automatically move there. For this setup, we'll use the compute shell we've just requested and start by choosing Python.

title: Make Python available in the compute shell
body:
Inside the allocation, in demo; use a version shown as available
module avail python
module load python/3.11.11
module list
CommandMeaning
module avail pythonList cluster modules matching Python
module load python/3.11.11Select this installed Python version for this shell
module listConfirm which cluster modules are loaded

analysis.py needs pandas. Next, create .venv in demo and install pandas there.
notes:
Before we install pandas, we need to know which Python we're installing it for. We're doing this inside the compute shell, in the remote demo folder.

The cluster already has software installations. The module command lets our shell select one of them. module avail python shows the available Python choices. module load python/3.11.11 selects the example version on this slide, and module list shows what's loaded.

The number after the slash is the version. We'd use a version that's actually available and keep that same compatible version in the batch script later.

Our analysis.py file uses pandas to read a table. pandas is a package, meaning reusable code that our program can load. Selecting Python doesn't automatically install that package for our project.

We'll give the project its own environment and install pandas there. You'll see Python's -m option in that command; it has a different meaning from the cluster's module command.

title: Create a Python environment and install pandas
body:
Continue in the same compute shell and remote demo folder
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install pandas
ls -a
Create .venv-m runs Python’s venv utility; .venv is the new folder.
Activatesource makes this shell use .venv/bin/python.
Install pandas-m pip runs the package installer for the selected Python.

ls -a shows the hidden .venv folder. After pip finishes, check the import on the next slide.
notes:
We'll stay in the same compute shell and demo folder, with the Python module loaded. The first command creates a folder called .venv for the project's environment.

In python -m venv .venv, -m tells Python to run a Python module as a program. venv is the environment tool, and the final .venv is the folder we're creating. The dot at the beginning makes it a hidden name in an ordinary listing.

source .venv/bin/activate then selects that environment for this shell. After activation, python points to .venv/bin/python. python -m pip install pandas runs the package installer through that selected Python, so pandas goes into this environment.

We wait for installation to finish and the prompt to return. ls -a includes hidden names, so it lets us see .venv in the project folder.

We're creating the environment on the cluster, rather than copying a laptop environment over. Activation only changes this shell; other terminals and jobs need to activate the same environment themselves. Before we rely on it, let's check that this Python can load pandas.

title: Check that pandas imports and save package versions
body:
-c executes the quoted Python code immediately
python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"
import pandasCheck that this Python can load the package.
Print versionprint(pandas.__version__) displays the installed version; expect a version number.
freeze lists versions; > writes the file, replacing existing contents
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt

Continue when a version prints without an error. Keep this compute shell open.
notes:
An installation finishing is useful, but what we really want to know is whether our Python can use the package. We're still in the same compute shell, with .venv active.

The -c option runs the Python code inside the quotes straight away. import pandas loads the package. The semicolon separates that instruction from print(pandas.__version__), which displays the installed version.

We're looking for a version number with no import error. If the import fails, we'd check the loaded Python module, environment activation, and any installation error before going further. A completed download alone doesn't prove that the package works.

Once that check passes, python -m pip freeze lists the installed package versions. The greater-than sign sends the list into requirements.txt. It replaces the file's existing contents if the file is already there. This saves a record of our packages; it doesn't install them again.

We'll keep this compute shell open briefly, because the diagram explains what stays after we close it.

title: The environment stays; activation is per shell
body:
Install packagespython -m pip install pandasAfter creating and activating .venv
Write files→
Shared project storage
demo/.venv/Python + installed packagesThese files remain.
Activate in each new shell or jobsource .venv/bin/activate
Current compute shell
python→.venv/bin/python
Same existing.venvNo reinstall
A later batch job
python→.venv/bin/python

After setup, exit returns to the login shell; .venv stays in project storage.
notes:
The useful way to think about this is that installation changes files, while activation changes what one shell uses.

At the top, python -m pip install pandas writes pandas and its dependencies into demo/.venv on shared project storage. Those files stay there when the compute shell closes.

At the bottom, source .venv/bin/activate tells a shell to use that existing environment. Its python command now points to .venv/bin/python. We're selecting an installation we already made. Activation doesn't request compute resources, and it doesn't select the environment in every other terminal or job.

A later batch job will load the same compatible Python module and activate this same .venv. Then, inside the program, import pandas loads the package so the code can use it. Creating the environment, activating it, and importing a package each have their own job.

Our setup is finished, so exit leaves this compute shell and releases the interactive allocation. hostname and pwd let us check that we're back on the login node in our project folder. If the allocation has already ended, check the host before typing exit again.

The .venv is ready to reuse. Before we put it in a batch script, here's an alternative you may encounter in another project: Conda.

title: Create a Conda environment from a supplied file
body:
Alternative to .venv; \ continues the command on the next line
module avail miniconda3
module load YOUR_CONDA_MODULE
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda run -n analysis \
  python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"
environment.ymlRecords the environment name and requested packages
-f environment.ymlRead the environment specification from this file.
-n analysisUse the environment named analysis (from name: analysis in the file).

Choose this instead of .venv. In a new compute shell, expect a pandas version with no error.
notes:
Sometimes a project comes with an environment.yml file. That file tells Conda the environment's name and which packages it needs. We'd choose this route instead of .venv; our main Python example doesn't need both.

The supplied environment.yml is in examples, so we'd first copy it into the remote project. We'd then request a new compute shell using the srun setup we just covered. This is its own setup session, after the earlier one has ended.

Conda may store environments in home. quota lets us check the space available before starting. If home is nearly full, we'd ask the group's technical contact where to put the environment.

module avail miniconda3 shows the available Conda modules. We'd replace YOUR_CONDA_MODULE with the actual module name to load. conda env create builds the environment, and -f tells it to read environment.yml. In our supplied file, the name is analysis.

conda run -n analysis runs the following command inside that named environment. The backslash continues the command on the next line, with nothing after the backslash. python -c runs the quoted import and version check, just as before. We'd expect a pandas version with no error.

After that optional setup, exit returns us to the login shell. For the rest of our main walkthrough, we'll use the .venv we've already prepared and put its setup in analysis.sbatch.

title: Prepare a Python batch job with its environment
body:
1 · Beginning of analysis.sbatch
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=analysis
#SBATCH --account=YOUR_ACCOUNT
#SBATCH --partition=YOUR_PARTITION
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=1G
#SBATCH --time=00:05:00
2 · Continue in the same file, after the left column
#SBATCH --output=analysis-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=analysis-%j.err

set -e
module load python/3.11.11
source .venv/bin/activate
python analysis.py

set -e stops on setup failure. Set your account and partition, then save analysis.sbatch.
notes:
Back in our main Python workflow, we have the package files in .venv. The batch job needs to select that environment when it starts.

These two columns are one analysis.sbatch file. The right column continues after the left. The first line, #!/bin/bash, selects Bash. All the #SBATCH settings come before the commands that run the program.

--job-name gives the job a label. --account and --partition need our approved allocation and queue. For this tiny example, --nodes, --ntasks, and --cpus-per-task request one node, one task, and one CPU for that task. --mem=1G requests one GiB of memory per node, and --time=00:05:00 sets a five-minute limit. A larger analysis needs settings that fit its own requirements.

--output and --error name the two logs. Slurm replaces %j with this job's ID. The supplied template also includes email settings, so we'd enter our own address or remove both email lines.

set -e stops this script if one of these setup commands fails. The job then loads the same available Python version we used during setup, activates .venv, and runs analysis.py. The packages are already there, so it reuses them.

We'll save analysis.sbatch in VS Code. Our login terminal is where we'll submit that saved file.

title: Submit the analysis job
body:
In the login shell, from the demo folder
pwd
ls data/samples.csv analysis.py analysis.sbatch
sbatch analysis.sbatch
Illustrative analysis job ID; hello used 123456
Submitted batch job 123457
Check whether this new job is pending or running
squeue -u YOUR_NETID

Use the returned ID in analysis-JOBID.out and analysis-JOBID.err.
notes:
We're ready to submit, but it's worth checking what the job will be able to find. In the login shell, pwd should show the remote demo folder. The ls command checks the input path, data/samples.csv, and our two script files, analysis.py and analysis.sbatch.

Then sbatch analysis.sbatch sends the saved batch file to Slurm. The response shown here is an illustrative job ID, 123457. We'd keep the number actually returned to us. It's a new job, separate from the earlier hello job.

squeue -u YOUR_NETID shows our jobs; -u selects the user whose jobs we want to see. It tells us whether this request is pending or running. Submission by itself doesn't mean the analysis has finished.

The returned ID also tells us which analysis-JOBID.out and analysis-JOBID.err files to open. They may not exist until the job starts. Once the output log is there, we can see what the program is reporting.

title: Follow job output with tail
body:
After the job starts and its log exists; use your actual job ID
tail -n 20 analysis-123457.out
tail -f analysis-123457.out

-n 20: show the last 20 lines · -f: keep following new output

Batch job 123457 Keeps running
writes→
Log fileanalysis-123457.out
read by→
Terminal log viewer tail -f
Ctrl+CStops viewing
The job and log viewer are separate processes.

To cancel the analysis job itself: scancel 123457.
notes:
We can watch the latest output without reopening the whole log each time. We'll use our actual job ID in the filename.

tail -n 20 shows the last twenty lines, then gives us the prompt back. tail -f keeps watching the file and displays new lines as they arrive. That's what the -f option does: follow the output.

The diagram separates the two things happening here. The batch job writes the log on the cluster. Our terminal runs tail to read that file. While tail -f is open, this terminal is occupied by the viewer.

Ctrl+C stops the viewer and gives us the prompt back. The submitted job keeps running. If we really wanted to cancel that job, we'd use scancel followed by its job ID. We don't need to cancel it just to stop watching.

With the prompt back, we can also look for problems in the error log.

title: Search the error log with grep
body:
After Ctrl+C stops the tail viewer; use your actual job ID
grep -in "error" analysis-123457.err
-iIgnore letter case: error also matches Error.
-nShow the matching line number.
Illustrative error: the matching message is on line 8
8:FileNotFoundError: data/samples.csv

Read the surrounding log. No match does not prove success; .err can also contain progress messages.
notes:
The error log can be long, so grep helps us find lines worth looking at. In this command, we're searching for the quoted text error inside analysis-123457.err, using our own job ID in practice.

-in combines two options. -i ignores letter case, so error also matches Error. -n adds the line number to each match.

This output is an illustration of a failed run. The 8 before the colon means the message is on line eight. FileNotFoundError tells us to investigate data/samples.csv. We'd open the log and read the surrounding lines, then check the working directory and path.

A search helps us locate text; it isn't a pass-or-fail test. No match, or even an empty error log, doesn't prove success. A nonempty .err file doesn't automatically mean failure either, because some programs write ordinary progress messages there.

After checking the job and its logs, we still need to inspect the actual result once the job has finished.

title: Open the result in VS Code
body:
Illustration · expected result from the supplied demo
EXPLORER · DEMO
▸ data
1 ▾ results2 summary.csvanalysis.py
analysis.sbatch
summary.csv
1samples,total_reads23,3700
3

3 input samples
3,700 total reads

Read it here. No download needed.
For a local copy: right-click the remote file → Download…

Other viewers: logs and images open directly;
Rainbow CSV colors columns; PDF/Jupyter extensions open those files.
notes:
For the result, we can return to the same VS Code Explorer we've been using. We'd refresh the folder if needed, expand results, and open summary.csv. We can read the remote file right there.

This illustration shows the expected result from the supplied demo. The header is samples,total_reads, followed by one summary row: 3,3700. That means three input samples and 3,700 total reads. The number of samples is the value in the first column; we're not expecting three output rows.

If the file is empty or incomplete, we'd return to the logs and check what happened. For our own projects, we'd also check that the contents make sense for the analysis, rather than treating a file's existence as proof that everything worked.

If we want a laptop copy, we can right-click the remote file and choose Download. Text and images open directly in VS Code. Rainbow CSV adds colors to table columns, while suitable PDF and Jupyter extensions let us open those file types. During installation, we'd follow the prompt for the local or SSH environment.

Opening a notebook doesn't reserve compute resources. We'd still check where its cells will run and keep substantial analysis off the login node.

That brings the Python workflow through to an expected result. For an R project, the Slurm routine stays very similar.

title: Run an R script as a Slurm batch job
body:
R commands below the #SBATCH resource settings
module load R
Rscript analysis.R
Copy analysis.R and analysis_R.sbatch into the project; set the account and partition
sbatch analysis_R.sbatch
Same inputdata/samples.csv
R outputresults/summary_R.csv

This example uses base R; no additional package installation is needed.
notes:
If your script is written in R, we keep the same pattern: prepare the files, submit a batch job, check the logs, and inspect the output. The part that changes is how we select R and run the script.

The examples folder contains analysis.R and analysis_R.sbatch. We'd copy both into the remote project that already has data/samples.csv, then set the approved account and partition in the batch file.

Below its #SBATCH resource settings, module load R selects the cluster's R installation. We'd use an R module name that's actually available. Rscript analysis.R runs the saved script directly, so an interactive R console isn't needed for this job.

This small example uses base R only. It doesn't need extra packages or a custom package library. If another script needs additional packages, we'd prepare them before submitting and make sure the job can use them.

From the login shell in that project, sbatch analysis_R.sbatch submits the job. It reads the same input table and writes results/summary_R.csv. We then follow the returned job ID through the queue, logs, and result, just as for Python.

If something goes wrong in either workflow, a few common messages give us a useful place to start.

title: Common errors and the first useful check
body:
What you seeCheck first
No such file or directoryRun pwd; check the path and filename capitalization.
Command not foundCheck spelling; load the module or activate the environment.
No module named… / no package called…Select the intended Python/R environment; install the missing package there.
OUT_OF_MEMORY / TIMEOUTCompare --mem / --time with the tool’s documented requirements.
Invalid account / partitionUse your approved --account and matching --partition.
Permission denied / quota exceededRun quota; confirm the group gave you write access to that folder.
notes:
When a job fails, I'd start with the message before submitting the same file again. It often points to a specific part of the setup.

For No such file or directory, pwd tells us where we're working. Then we'd check the path, spelling, and capital letters. For Command not found, we'd check spelling and whether the right module or environment is selected. A missing Python or R package means checking which environment the job actually uses and installing the package there.

OUT_OF_MEMORY means the job exceeded its memory allowance. TIMEOUT means it reached its time limit. We'd look at the log and the software's requirements, then review --mem or --time accordingly.

An invalid account or partition means checking that --account and --partition are an approved pair. For a quota error, quota shows usage and limits. Permission denied is a reason to check that our group has given us write access to the folder.

If we need help, the job ID, batch script, exact error, and software version give someone a concrete starting point. We don't need to send a password or the whole dataset. The official guide and ICC support are good places to turn when we need more help.

You don't need to remember every command from today. These links are here so you can find the details when you're setting up your own work.

I'd start with the ICC guide for this cluster's accounts, storage, software, and job submission. Missing Semester explains the shell ideas behind the commands. The Microsoft, Slurm, and package documentation helps with the editor, individual options, and software environments.

For an account-specific problem, ICC support can check details that a general tutorial can't. The address is on this slide. Including the job ID, exact error, relevant batch file, and software version makes it easier to help.

The workflow we've walked through is the same one we'll use for a larger analysis: connect, choose the project folder, prepare the software, request resources, submit the saved script, and check the logs and result. Our examples are deliberately small. For a real project, we'd replace the placeholders and choose the software versions and resources that the analysis needs.

That should give you a practical starting point for using the Campus Cluster. Thanks, everyone.
